summary: Introduces DepBench, 95 real dependency-upgrade PRs (Maven 38, npm 33, Cargo 15, PyPI 9; 10 libraries such as JUnit 4->5 and Spring Boot 2.7->3.0) with Docker oracles running the consumer's own tests, and DepRepair, a single-call pipeline that distills upstream changelogs/diffs into old->new migration rules, greps consumer usage sites, and adds breaking-change-type guidance. DepRepair reaches 89.5% (GPT-5.5) and 82.1% (Opus 4.6), significantly above a plain single-call prompt but statistically tied with Codex CLI / Claude Code given no upstream evidence; feeding agents the raw changelog drops them 13.7-23.2 pp.

claims.claim: DepRepair attains the highest pass rate on each backbone (89.5% GPT-5.5, 82.1% Opus 4.6)
claims.evidence: Table III: 85/95 and 78/95; McNemar shows significance vs Direct LLM (+7, p=0.016; +10, p=0.002) but NOT vs Codex minimal (87.4%) or Claude Code minimal (81.1%), gaps of 2 and 1 instances. Authors concede 'on par'. Conclusion still says 'ranking ahead of state-of-the-art coding agents'.

claims.claim: Raw upstream evidence reduces LLM and agent pass rates by 7-23 pp
claims.evidence: Table V: -7.4 (Direct GPT), -13.7 (Codex), -10.5 (Direct Opus), -23.2 (Claude Code); single temperature-0 run per configuration, McNemar p<0.001 vs DepRepair for agents.

claims.claim: Structured evidence consistently improves LLMs and agents
claims.evidence: Agents were never given structured evidence (§V-B), so the agent half is unsupported; ablation Table VI on Opus shows rules+locator without subcategory guidance, or guidance without rules, both fall to 61.1%, below the 71.6% no-evidence baseline, contradicting 'consistently'.

claims.claim: Empty patches, not wrong patches, are the dominant failure; DepRepair cuts them to 10/95
claims.evidence: Table IV: DepRepair 10, Direct minimal 21, Codex minimal 21, Direct upstream 32, Claude Code minimal 35; on GPT-5.5 every emitted DepRepair diff passed.

claims.claim: Paradigm shifts remain hardest (65-70%); import migration saturated (100% for all)
claims.evidence: Table VII; DepRepair GPT-5.5 solves all 38 Maven instances.

patterns.note: Treats upstream library + consumer as a cross-repository problem; distilled upstream rules beat raw upstream text.

LLM-distilled old->new migration rules plus usage scan act like a soft recipe; the paper never compares to OpenRewrite-style deterministic recipes, and import migrations (which recipes handle) were already 100% for all methods.
Usage locator is a lexical scan for imports/call sites of changed symbols; part of the full pipeline that reduces empty patches.
Distilling noisy changelogs into compact rules outperforms dumping raw evidence into context, which actively hurts agents.
Execution oracle used only for post-hoc grading; all methods denied in-loop build/test, so verifier loops were not tested.

methodology.sample: 95 instances from 10 library major-version transitions in 4 ecosystems; uneven (PyPI 9, paradigm shift 20)
methodology.baselines: Direct single-call LLM (minimal/upstream), Codex CLI and Claude Code (minimal/upstream); agents run without in-loop build/test, which removes their main advantage; no deterministic migration tool (e.g., OpenRewrite, Renovate-style recipes) or prior breaking-change repair system compared
methodology.variance: single run per configuration, no retries; McNemar/Fisher paired tests reported
methodology.ablations: component ablation on both backbones (Table VI)
methodology.contamination_controls: none; gold patches are public GitHub PRs for very well-known migrations (JUnit 5, Spring Boot 3, Vue 3, Pydantic 2) likely in training data

standards.artifacts: no code or benchmark release link found in text; subcategory labels said to be 'released for scrutiny' without location

biases.detail: Popular public migrations and their PRs predate model cutoffs; no temporal split or contamination check.
Coding agents deprived of build/test feedback during generation, and given only raw (not structured) evidence; no deterministic recipe baseline.
Authors' own benchmark and taxonomy (author-assigned subcategory labels) used to evaluate authors' own method.
Single temperature-0 run per configuration; agents are stochastic even at temperature 0.
No released benchmark or code link in the paper.
95 instances; authors note limited power, per-cell rates rest on 9-27 instances.
Contributions claim 'a fraction of their cost' vs agents but no cost/token table was found in the evaluated sections.

coi.affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University (first author, work done during Microsoft internship); Microsoft (remaining seven authors)
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: GPT-5.5 / Codex CLI (OpenAI, Microsoft partner) and Claude Opus 4.6 / Claude Code (Anthropic) as backbones and baselines; no Microsoft product is the subject
coi.detail: Vendor-affiliated authors, but the evaluated method is a research prototype and both third-party backbones are treated symmetrically.

verdict_reason: Executable oracle, two backbones, paired significance tests and an honest 'on par with agents' reading; but single runs, no artifact release, contamination-prone public migrations, agents handicapped by no in-loop tests, and an abstract claim (structured evidence improves agents) that was never tested and is contradicted by the Opus ablation.
applicability: Highly relevant to a Java backend team: Spring Boot 2.7->3.0 and JUnit 4->5 are in the benchmark and DepRepair solved all 38 Maven instances. Practical takeaway for the harness: when an ingestion repo upgrades a dependency (or when one of the >=4 ingestion repos changes a shared library API consumed by others), do not paste raw release notes into the agent; first distill them into explicit old->new rules, grep the consumer repos for affected sites, and hand the agent that structured brief. This fits spec-driven development (the rules file is the spec). Do not drop build/test in the loop just because the paper did; and for mechanical renames/imports prefer deterministic OpenRewrite recipes, which the paper never compared against. Host-agnostic: the brief works for any agent host.
